lines.text: Loose stools containing visible blood are a key presenting feature to assess.
A haemoglobin below 10.5 g/dL counts as a marker of systemic toxicity.
A calprotectin above 50 ug/g supports referral in adults with recent-onset lower gastrointestinal symptoms.
Consider inflammatory bowel disease as a working diagnosis when symptoms and raised inflammatory markers suggest it.
Base confirmation on combined clinical, laboratory, endoscopic and histological findings together, after exclusion of other causes.
Ulcerative colitis is continuous mucosal inflammation starting in the rectum and extending variably up the colon, with extent and severity guiding treatment.
Send stool culture when this condition is suspected and with every flare to exclude other causes.
Use colonoscopy with biopsy with samples from the terminal ileum and each colonic segment to establish the diagnosis and distinguish subtypes.
Record disease extent by maximal involvement as E1, E2 or E3.
Assess truelove and witts severity as mild, moderate or severe; severe cases require hospital admission.
Extensive disease extends beyond the splenic flexure and includes pancolitis.
Severe acute presentation is a medical emergency requiring admission with joint medical and surgical input and early planning for rescue therapy.
Hospital treatment for this presentation is categorized as Tier 2.
Give hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously four times daily until response is assessed on day 3.
Alternatively, give methylprednisolone 60 mg intravenously once daily until response is assessed on day 3.
If intravenous steroids fail, rescue therapy or colectomy is considered, categorized as Tier 3.
Record stool frequency each day, with formal review on day 3; more than 8 per day predicts colectomy is likely.
Check CRP each day, with formal review on day 3; above 45 mg/L predicts colectomy is likely.
On day 3, more than 8 per day means no response, so discuss rescue therapy or surgery.
On day 3, CRP above 45 mg/L means no response, so discuss rescue therapy or surgery.
No specific diet has been shown to bring on or sustain remission.
Screen for malnutrition and provide individualized dietary advice.
New or worsening bloody diarrhoea should be checked to exclude infection before escalating treatment.
Colonic dilatation with signs of systemic toxicity is a surgical emergency needing urgent joint medical and surgical review.
Hospital admission with active disease carries higher clot risk, so give pharmacological prophylaxis unless contraindicated, even with rectal bleeding.
Persistent dilatation with toxicity, perforation or major bleeding are triggers for emergency colectomy.
Visible blood in loose stools is a key presenting feature to assess.
A haemoglobin below 10.5 g/dL counts as a marker of systemic toxicity.
Faecal calprotectin above 50 ug/g supports referral to look for inflammatory bowel disease.
When inflammatory bowel disease is suspected, stool culture should be sent to exclude infection.
Colonoscopy with biopsy with biopsies from each segment is the key test to establish ulcerative colitis.
Acute severe ulcerative colitis is a medical emergency needing admission with joint medical and surgical care.
Hydrocortisone 100 mg given intravenously four times daily is a first-line steroid regimen.
Methylprednisolone 60 mg given intravenously once daily is an alternative steroid regimen.
Recorded stool frequency above 8 per day predicts that colectomy is likely.
A CRP above 45 mg/L with ongoing stools predicts that colectomy is likely.
After primary non-response, loss of response or intolerance to anti-TNF therapy, check trough levels and anti-drug antibodies to guide the next step; this is a tier 3 pathway.
With adequate levels, change to another class such as ustekinumab, vedolizumab or tofacitinib.
With low levels or antibodies after loss of response, optimising or changing to a second anti-TNF can be supported.
Ustekinumab maintenance is 90 mg given under the skin every 8 weeks after a single weight-based intravenous induction dose, continued while the patient responds.
Vedolizumab is given as 300 mg by infusion at weeks 0, 2 and 6, then every 8 weeks, continued while the patient responds.
Tofacitinib induction is 10 mg taken orally twice daily for 8 weeks, followed by a lower maintenance dose once the colitis responds.
When response is lost, reactive testing helps guide the next step, aiming for a trough of at least 5 ug/mL.
An intermediate treatment target is a fall to 250 ug/g or below.
Before starting anti-TNF or other biologic therapy, screen for latent tuberculosis and hepatitis B and review vaccination status.
When colitis is responding to corticosteroids during a switch, use them only as a short bridge until the new maintenance treatment takes effect, then taper them off.

notices: Noted treatment history: infliximab — no response; corticosteroid — responded.
